doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Bop's short life, Dizzy Gillespie at Lincoln Center and durable classics
summary: Murray says bop and cool had short lives yet people treat them as new, recalls John Lewis and Carnegie Hall in 1947, and says Basie could still play his Kansas City material.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: So by 1942 or 3, by 1955 they were talking about “cool.” You know what I mean? That’s a very short life. Although some people, now, got stuck in that, and they act like bop was day before yesterday. Like the guys — we hear that Dizzy Gillespie broke up at Lincoln Center last month, well early this month, this is still September, yeah? Yeah, earlier this month. It opened the season, and now people are acting as if that was yesterday. And John Lewis and I were talking about them playing the big — the band stuff, the full band stuff. And I would say I was at Carnegie Hall that night and when he played so-and-so he’d say “yeah man, do you realize that that was 50 years ago?” That was 1947.
I was in graduate school. And these guys act like that’s the latest thing. And it’s much older than King Oliver was when they were playing bop. King Oliver was still playing in the 1930s, right?
It’s amazing how fast jazz has moved, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

Well the time has gotten there. There’s a lot of fluctuations and interests and so forth, but the durable things are still there because they’re still — like Basie you see? He could play stuff that he played, see that’s the test of art. Can you play stuff that you played when you first came out of Kansas City. He could. I’m sure the last thing he played was “Jumpin’ at the Woodside.”

Yeah. Because the quality, you understand, the quality is durable. And that’s where the security comes in, you see. If you’ve got something you’re betting your life on today, then tomorrow it’s out of style, then that’s like trying to embrace entropy instead of making a bulwark against entropy. That’s the big problem.
